title: Of the battle of Dreux
paragraphs: [December 19, 1562, in which the Catholics, under the command of the Duc de Guise and the Constable de Montmorency, defeated the Protestants, commanded by the Prince de Conde. See Sismondi, Hist. des Francais, vol. xviii., p. 354.]

Our battle of Dreux is striking for several extraordinary incidents — though those who have little affection for M. de Guise, and care little for his reputation, are eager to blame him. They say his halt, his delay with the forces under his command while the Constable, who was general of the army, was being raked through and through by the enemy's artillery, his battalion routed, himself taken prisoner — is inexcusable. He would have done much better, they argue, to risk a flank charge than to wait for the chance to fall on the enemy's rear, and so suffer such a heavy and consequential loss. But quite apart from what the outcome later showed, anyone who weighs the case without passion or prejudice will readily admit that the aim of a captain — and indeed of every private soldier — should be the overall victory, and that no particular incident, however close to his own interest, should pull him from that pursuit. Philopoemen, in an encounter with Machanidas, had sent out a strong party of his archers and slingers to open the skirmish. They were routed and hotly pursued by the enemy, who, riding their luck and chasing the rout, swept past the battalion where Philopoemen was stationed. His own men were straining to attack, but he refused to leave his post or to expose himself to relieve them. He let his archers be cut down before his eyes, and then, when he saw the enemy foot left unprotected by their cavalry, charged in. Even though they were Lacedaemonians, he caught them at the very moment when, thinking the victory secured, they were beginning to break their ranks. He destroyed them with ease and then set off in pursuit of Machanidas. The case is very like Monsieur de Guise's.

In that bloody clash between Agesilaus and the Boeotians — which Xenophon, who was there, calls the sharpest fight he ever saw — Agesilaus turned down the advantage fortune had set in front of him: to let the Boeotian battalions march past and then charge them in the rear. Even though he could have counted on victory, he judged this would smell more of cunning than of courage. To show his prowess, he chose instead, with marvellous fire, to charge them head-on. He was badly beaten and badly wounded for his pains, and at last had to disengage and take the very course he had first refused — opening his battalion to let the Boeotian torrent through. When they had passed and he noticed they were marching in disorder, like men who thought themselves safe, he pursued them and struck their flank. Even then he could not turn it into a full rout: they retreated at their leisure, keeping their faces toward him, until they reached safety.

title: Of names
paragraphs: Whatever variety of herbs are tossed together in the dish, the whole mass goes down under the single name of a salad. In the same way, under the heading of names, I am going to throw together a hodge-podge of several different items.

Every nation has certain names that, for reasons I cannot quite explain, are taken in no good sense — with us, for example, John, William, Benedict. In the genealogies of princes, too, certain names seem fatally attached: the Ptolemies of Egypt, the Henries in England, the Charleses in France, the Baldwins in Flanders, the Williams of our old Aquitaine — from which, they say, the name Guyenne is derived. That derivation would seem far-fetched if there were not derivations just as crude in Plato himself.

Another item: a frivolous thing in itself, but worth recording for its strangeness, written down by an eyewitness — that Henry, Duke of Normandy, son of Henry II, king of England, threw a great feast in France. The crowd of nobility and gentry was so dense that, for sport, they were divided into companies by name. In the first company, made up of Williams, there were a hundred and ten knights of that name seated at table, not counting the ordinary gentlemen and servants.

It is as amusing to sort the tables by the guests' names as it was for the Emperor Geta to sort the courses of his meal by the first letters of the dishes themselves — so that everything starting with B was served together: brawn, beef, bream, bustards, becca-ficos, and so on. Another item: there is a saying that it is good to have a good name, meaning credit and a good reputation. But beyond that, it is genuinely useful to have a well-sounding name — easy to pronounce, easy to remember — because kings and other great people will then more easily recognise us and more reluctantly forget us. Even among our own servants, we tend to call and employ the ones whose names come most readily to the tongue. I myself saw Henry II, when for the life of him he could not call up the name of a gentleman from our country of Gascony, fall back on calling one of the queen's maids of honour by the general name of her family because her own name was so hard to pronounce or remember. And Socrates thinks it worth a father's care to give his children fine names.

Another item: it is said that Notre Dame la Grande at Poitiers was founded for this reason — that a debauched young man living in the area got hold of a girl, and at her first arrival asked her name. When she said "Mary," he was so suddenly pierced through by the awe of religion and the reverence due to that sacred name of the Blessed Virgin that he not only sent the girl away at once but reformed his life and lived the rest of it that way. In commemoration of this miracle, a chapel to Our Lady was raised on the spot where his house had stood, and later the church that we see there today. That correction worked through the ear, right into the soul. The one that follows worked simply through the senses. Pythagoras, in company with some wild young men, saw that, heated by the feast, they were plotting to break into a respectable household. He ordered the singing girl to drop her wanton melodies, and with a solemn, grave, spondaic music gently disenchanted and lulled their ardour to sleep.

Another item: will not later generations say that our modern reformation has been wonderfully delicate and exact — not only fighting errors and vices and filling the world with devotion, humility, obedience, peace, and every virtue, but going so far as to pick a quarrel with our old baptismal names of Charles, Louis, Francis, in order to fill the world with Methuselahs, Ezekiels, and Malachis, names of a more spiritual ring? A gentleman who is a neighbour of mine, a great admirer of antiquity, always praising former ages above this present one of ours, among the rest never forgot to dwell on the lofty, magnificent sound of the gentlemen's names of those days — Don Grumedan, Quedregan, Agesilan — which, just to hear named, he felt denoted a different sort of man from Pierre, Guillot, and Michel.

Another item: I am thoroughly pleased with Jacques Amyot for leaving the Latin names intact throughout a French oration, without distorting them to fit a French cadence. It seemed a bit harsh and rough at first, but custom, on the authority of his Plutarch, has already overcome that novelty. I have often wished those who write history in Latin would leave our names as they find them. Turning Vaudemont into Vallemontanus, twisting names to make them match the Greek or Latin — we lose our bearings, and along with the men themselves we lose the benefit of the story.

To wrap it up: there is a wretched custom of bad consequence in our kingdom of France of calling every man by the name of his manor or seigneury. There is nothing in the world that more confounds families and bloodlines. A younger son of a good family, given a manor by his father and known and honoured by its name, can hardly drop it; ten years after his death the property passes into the hands of a stranger, who does the same — and just try to keep track of who these men are. We need look no further than our own royal family, where every partition creates a new surname, while the original family name is completely lost. The liberty taken in these changes is so great that in my time I have not seen a single man raised by fortune to any unusual rank who did not immediately have genealogical titles tacked on, new and unknown to his father, grafted onto some illustrious stem by sheer luck. And the murkiest families are the most willing to forge. How many gentlemen do we have in France who claim royal descent? More, I think, than will admit they do not. Was it not a delightful turn from a friend of mine? A group of gentlemen had gathered to debate the dispute between two seigneurs, one of whom genuinely had more impressive titles and alliances than the ordinary nobility. As the case was argued, every man, to put himself on a level with him, alleged some claim — one cited a particular descent, another a near resemblance of name, another a similarity of arms, another an old worm-eaten patent; the very least of them was great-grandchild to some foreign king. When they sat down to dinner, my friend, rather than take his place among them, withdrew with the most ceremonious bows and begged the company to excuse him for having until now lived among them with the impudence of a peer. Now that he understood their true quality, he said, he would begin to pay them the respect their birth and grandeur deserved, and that it would ill become him to sit down at the same table with so many princes — ending the farce with a thousand barbs: "Let us, for God's sake, be content with what our fathers were content with, and with what we are. We are great enough, if we know how to keep it. Let us not disown the rank and condition of our ancestors, and let us put away these ridiculous pretensions, which are never lacking to anyone shameless enough to put them forward."

Coats of arms have no more security than surnames. I carry azure powdered with trefoils or, with a lion's paw of the same armed gules in fess. What privilege has it to stay particularly in my house? A son-in-law will carry it off into another family; some shabby purchaser will take it for his own first arms. There is nothing in which there is more change and confusion.

But this thought drags me, against my will, onto another topic. Let us look a little closer at — and, for God's sake, examine — the foundation on which we build this glory and reputation for which the world is turned upside down. What do we mean by this renown we hunt after with such effort? In the end it is Peter or William who carries it, takes it as his own, and whom it alone concerns. What a brave faculty hope is — in a mortal subject, and in a moment, it thinks nothing of laying hold of infinity, immensity, eternity, and of stocking its master's poverty, at will, with anything he can imagine or desire! Nature has given us this passion as a pretty toy to play with. And this Peter or William — what is it, when all is said and done? A sound, or three or four strokes of the pen, so easy to vary that I would love to know to whom the glory of so many victories should be assigned: Guesquin? Glesquin? Gueaquin? And yet there is more at stake here than in Lucian, where Sigma sues Tau in court; for —
"Non levia aut ludicra petuntur Praemia;"
["They aim at no slight or jocular rewards."--AEneid, xii. 764.]

the chase here is very much in earnest: which of these letters is to be rewarded for so many sieges, battles, wounds, imprisonments, and services rendered to the crown of France by this famous constable? Nicholas Denisot never bothered himself with anything beyond the letters of his name, whose order he scrambled to build up by anagram the Count d'Alsinois, on whom he handsomely settled the glory of his own poetry and painting. The historian Suetonius was satisfied with just the sense of his name, and dropped his father's surname Lenis to leave Tranquillus as heir to his reputation. Who would believe that Captain Bayard has no honour but what he derives from the deeds of Peter Terrail; or that Antonio Iscalin should sit and watch himself robbed, to his face, of the honour of so many sea voyages and commands by sea and land under the names of Captain Paulin and the Baron de la Garde? Second, these strokes of the pen are common to thousands of people. How many in each family share the same name and surname? And how many more in different families, ages, and countries? History tells us of three Socrateses, five Platos, eight Aristotles, seven Xenophons, twenty Demetrii, twenty Theodores — and we can guess how many more she never met. What is to stop my stable-boy from calling himself Pompey the Great? But when all is done, what virtue, what authority, what secret machinery is there that pins onto my dead stable-boy, or onto the other Pompey whose head was cut off in Egypt, this glorious renown and these so honoured flourishes of the pen, to their advantage?
"Id cinerem et manes credis curare sepultos?"
["Do you believe the dead regard such things?"--AEneid, iv. 34.]
What does it mean to the two men I most admire, Epaminondas, of this fine verse that has gone round so many ages in his honour,
"Consiliis nostris laus est attrita Laconum;"
["The glory of the Spartans is extinguished by my plans."--Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 17.]
or to Africanus, of this other,
"A sole exoriente supra Maeotis Paludes Nemo est qui factis me aequiparare queat."
["From where the sun rises over the Palus Maeotis, to where it sets, there is no one whose acts can compare with mine."--Idem, ibid.]

Survivors tickle themselves with these fine phrases, and goaded by them into envy and longing, attribute, thoughtlessly and according to their own fancy, this feeling of theirs to the dead — vainly flattering themselves that one day in turn they will be capable of the same praise. Even so:
"Ad haec se Romanus Graiusque, et Barbaras induperator Erexit; caucus discriminis atque laboris Inde habuit: tanto major famae sitis est, quam Virtutis."

["For these the Roman, the Greek, and the Barbarian commander hath aroused himself; he has incurred thence causes of danger and toil: so much greater is the thirst for fame than for virtue."--Juvenal, x. 137.]

title: Of the uncertainty of our judgment
paragraphs: Well said is this line:
["There is everywhere much liberty of speech."--Iliad, xx. 249.]
For example:
["Hannibal conquered, but knew not how to make the best use of his victorious venture."--Petrarch, Son., 83.]

Anyone wanting to develop this point — to condemn our commanders' failure to press home the victory at Moncontour, or to accuse the King of Spain of not knowing how to make the most of his advantage over us at St. Quentin — may put these lapses down to a soul already drunk with success, or to a spirit so full and overstuffed with the start of good fortune that it has lost the appetite for adding to it, having quite enough on its plate to digest what it has already swallowed. He has his arms full and can hold no more; he is unworthy of the benefit fortune has handed him and of the advantage she has placed in his hand. For what good does it do him if he nonetheless gives his enemy time to regroup and rally? What chance is there that he will dare another day to attack an enemy reunited, reorganised, and freshly armed with anger and revenge — when he did not dare pursue them while they were routed and unmanned by fear?
"Dum fortuna calet, dum conficit omnia terror."
["Whilst fortune is fresh, and terror finishes all."--Lucan, vii. 734.]

But for all that, what better chance can he expect than the one he has thrown away? This is not fencing, where the most hits wins the prize; for as long as the enemy is on his feet, the game has to start over, and a victory that does not put an end to the war is not properly a victory at all. In the engagement where Caesar came off worst, near the city of Oricum, he taunted Pompey's soldiers by saying he would have been lost had their general known how to win. He paid Pompey back in a very different way when his own turn came.

But why might one not also argue the opposite — that it is the mark of a hasty and insatiable spirit not to know how to bound and restrain its appetite; that to exceed the measure God has set on his favours is to abuse them; and that to fling yourself back into danger after a victory is to put yourself a second time at the mercy of fortune; that one of the great pieces of discretion in war is not to drive an enemy to despair? Sulla and Marius, in the Social War, after defeating the Marsians, saw a reserve body still coming on, goaded by despair like maddened beasts, and judged it not wise to take their charge. Had Monsieur de Foix's ardour not carried him so furiously after the remains of the victory at Ravenna, he would not have darkened it with his own death. And the fresh memory of his example saved Monsieur d'Anguien from the same misfortune at the battle of Serisoles. It is dangerous to press a man for whom you have left no way out except his weapons, for necessity teaches violent decisions:
"Gravissimi sunt morsus irritatae necessitatis."
["Irritated necessity bites deepest."--Portius Latro., Declam.]
"Vincitur haud gratis, jugulo qui provocat hostem."
["He is not readily beaten who provokes the enemy by shewing his throat."--or: "He who presents himself to his foe, sells his life dear."--Lucan, iv. 275.]

This is what made Pharax hold back the King of Lacedaemon, who had just won a battle against the Mantineans, from charging a thousand Argians who had escaped in a body from the defeat — better, he thought, to let them slip off freely than to meet valour sharpened and enraged by misfortune. Clodomir, king of Aquitaine, after his victory pursued Gondemar, king of Burgundy, who was beaten and making off as fast as he could for safety; he forced him to turn and face him, and that stubbornness cost Clodomir the fruit of his conquest, for he lost his life there.

In the same way, if one had to decide whether soldiers should be lavishly and sumptuously dressed or armed only as the immediate task requires, the argument for the first might run as follows — and Sertorius, Philopoemen, Brutus, Caesar, and others held this view: that fine attire inflames a soldier's courage and is a spur to him; and that it also makes him fight more stubbornly, since his arms are in effect his estate and his whole inheritance to defend. This is why, says Xenophon, the men of Asia carried their wives and concubines, with their best jewels and richest possessions, with them to the wars. But the arguments would line up just as readily on the other side: that a general ought to reduce, not enlarge, his men's anxiety about saving themselves; that fine equipment makes them doubly afraid to risk their persons, and serves as a double temptation to the enemy to fight more resolutely where such booty and rich spoils are to be had. The thing was famously observed in earlier times as a powerful incentive to the Romans against the Samnites. Antiochus, showing Hannibal the army he had raised — marvellously splendid and rich in every kind of equipage — asked him whether the Romans would be satisfied with that army. "Satisfied?" replied Hannibal. "Yes, no doubt — however great their greed." Lycurgus not only forbade his soldiers all manner of finery in their gear but also forbade them to strip the enemies they defeated, because he wanted, as he said, poverty and frugality to shine alongside the rest of the battle.

At sieges and on other occasions where we come up close to the enemy, we readily let our men taunt, abuse, and revile him with every kind of injurious language. There is some colour of reason in this: it is no small thing to strip them of all hope of mercy or terms by reminding them that no quarter is to be expected from an enemy they have provoked so far, and that no remedy is left except victory. And yet Vitellius found himself fooled by this approach. He had to deal with Otho's soldiers, who were weaker in valour, long unused to war and softened by the pleasures of Rome. He stung them at last with so much abuse — reproaching them with cowardice and with regret for the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind in the city — that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation could have produced, and made them fall upon him with a fury their own captains had been unable to rouse in them. And indeed, when the injuries cut to the quick, it can easily happen that the man who was going reluctantly to fight on his prince's behalf will pitch in with another kind of spirit when the quarrel becomes his own.

Considering how important it is to keep the general of an army alive, and that the enemy's whole aim is directed straight at the head on which all the rest depend, the course taken by so many great captains — changing their dress and disguising themselves just before engaging — seems past dispute. And yet the inconvenience a man runs into by doing so is no less than the one he thinks to avoid. The captain, hidden from the recognition of his own men, no longer has the courage his presence and example would have inspired in them; not seeing the familiar marks and ensigns of their leader, they soon conclude that either he is dead or, despairing of the business, has gone off to look after himself. And experience shows both methods have succeeded and failed. What happened to Pyrrhus in the battle he fought against the Consul Levinus in Italy will serve to illustrate both points. By hiding himself in Megacles's armour and giving Megacles his own, he undoubtedly saved his life — but by that very means he came very close to the other disaster of losing the battle. Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus loved to be recognisable in a fight by rich equipment and armour of a particular gleam and colour. Agis, Agesilaus, and that great Gilippus, on the contrary, used to fight without any display, with no imperial escort or distinguishing marks.

Among the other faults laid to Pompey's charge at Pharsalia, he is reproached for keeping his army standing still to receive the enemy's charge — "because by doing so" (I will here lift Plutarch's own words, which are better than mine) "he deprived himself of the violent impact that running adds to the first shock of arms, and he prevented that crash of the combatants into one another that usually gives them greater impetuosity and fury, especially when they rush in with full force, their courage rising with the shouts and the run. He chilled the soldiers' ardour, as it were, and made it more reserved." That is what Plutarch says. But if Caesar had come off worse, why might not someone else have argued the reverse — that the strongest and steadiest fighting stance is one in which a man is planted firm, without motion; that those who hold steady on the march, closing up and reserving their strength for the moment of action, have a great advantage over men who are disordered, who have already spent half their breath running headlong into the charge. Besides, an army is a body made up of so many individual members that it is impossible for it to move at that pace without breaking the order of battle, and without the leading men being engaged before their comrades can come up to help them. In that unnatural battle between the two Persian brothers, the Lacedaemonian Clearchus, who commanded the Greeks on Cyrus's side, led them on softly and without haste toward the charge, but when they were within fifty paces he hurled them on at full speed, hoping in so short a run to keep order and save their wind and at the same time to give weight and impetus both to their persons and to their missile weapons. Others have settled the question for their own armies this way: if your enemy comes at you full tilt, stand firm to receive him; if he stands still to receive you, charge him full tilt.

When the Emperor Charles V invaded Provence, King Francis had to choose between going to meet him in Italy or waiting for him on his own ground. He weighed how much it mattered to keep his own territory intact and free from the troubles of war, so that, with its resources unspent, it could go on supplying men and money as needed; and that war requires constantly laying waste the country before you, which is not something easily done at home. Add to this that country people swallow such damage less easily from their own side than from an enemy, so that mutinies and uprisings could be sparked among us; that the licence of pillage and plunder, intolerable at home, is a great relief and refreshment from the strains and miseries of war; that a man who has nothing to look forward to but his bare pay will hardly be kept from running home when he is two steps from his wife and his own door; that the man who lays the cloth always pays for the feast; that there is more alacrity in attacking than in defending; and that the shock of a lost battle in one's own bowels is so violent it threatens to throw the whole body out of joint, no passion being as contagious as fear, none so readily believed, none so suddenly spread; and that cities hearing this tempest rattling at their gates, taking in their captains and soldiers still panting and trembling, would be in danger, in the heat and rush of the moment, of throwing themselves at some rash resolution. Yet despite all this, he chose to recall the forces he had beyond the mountains and let the enemy come to him. For he could, on the other hand, suppose that being at home and among friends, he could not fail of every kind of convenience; the rivers and passes were at his disposal and could bring him supplies and money in safety, with no trouble of convoy; he would find his subjects all the more devoted to him the closer the danger pressed; with so many cities and barriers behind him to secure him, it would be in his power to dictate the time and place of battle to suit himself; and if he chose to delay, then quietly and at his ease he could watch his enemy founder and defeat himself with the difficulties he was bound to encounter — engaged in hostile country, with war made on him from in front, from behind, and from every side; no way to refresh himself or expand his quarters should disease set in; nowhere safe to lodge his wounded; no money and no provisions except at the point of the lance; no leisure to rest and catch his breath; no knowledge of the country or the roads to keep him safe from ambushes and surprises; and in case of a lost battle, no possible way of saving the remnants. And there are plenty of examples for either course.

Scipio thought it much better to attack his enemy's territory in Africa than to stay at home defending his own and fighting Hannibal in Italy, and it worked out well for him. But in the same war, on the other hand, Hannibal ruined himself by giving up the conquest of a foreign country to go and defend his own. The Athenians, leaving the enemy in their own territory to cross into Sicily, were not favoured by fortune in that plan; but Agathocles, king of Syracuse, found her favourable when he crossed into Africa and left the war behind at home.

From such examples we usually conclude, and with some reason, that events, especially in war, mostly depend on fortune, who will not be governed by, nor submit to, human reasoning and prudence — as the poet has it:

"Et male consultis pretium est: prudentia fallit Nec fortune probat causas, sequiturque merentes, Sed vaga per cunctos nullo discrimine fertur. Scilicet est aliud, quod nos cogatque regatque Majus, et in proprias ducat mortalia leges."

["And there is value in ill counsel: prudence deceives: nor does fortune inquire into causes, nor aid the most deserving, but turns hither and thither without discrimination. Indeed there is a greater power which directs and rules us, and brings mortal affairs under its own laws."--Manilius, iv. 95.]

But, to take the matter properly, it would seem that our deliberations and decisions depend just as much on fortune as anything else we do, and that she catches our reasoning too up in her uncertainty and confusion. "We argue rashly and at a venture," says Timaeus in Plato, "because, like us, our reasoning shares heavily in the rashness of chance."

title: Of war horses, or destriers
paragraphs: Here I have turned grammarian — I, who never learned any language except by ear, and who still do not know adjective from conjunction or ablative. I think I have read that the Romans had a class of horses they called funales or dextrarios, which were either led horses, or relay horses posted at intervals to be picked up fresh as needed; and that is why we call our service horses destriers, and our romances commonly use adestrer for accompagner, to accompany. They also gave the name desultorios equos to horses trained so well that, running at full speed side by side without bridle or saddle, the Roman gentlemen, armed at all points, could swing themselves over from one to the other. The Numidian men-at-arms always had a led horse along beside the one they rode, ready to change in the heat of battle:
"Quibus, desultorum in modum, binos trahentibus equos, inter acerrimam saepe pugnam, in recentem equum, ex fesso, armatis transultare mos erat: tanta velocitas ipsis, tamque docile equorum genus."
["To whom it was a custom, leading along two horses, often in the hottest fight, to leap armed from a tired horse to a fresh one; so active were the men, and the horses so docile."--Livy, xxiii. 29.]

There are many horses trained to help their riders so well that they will rush at anyone who shows a drawn sword, and fall on whoever faces or opposes them with mouth and hoofs. But they often do more harm to their friends than to their enemies; and once they are engaged and locked on you cannot get them off and back into order, so that you are left at the mercy of their fight. It went very badly for Artybius, general of the Persian army, in a single combat with Onesilus, king of Salamis, to be mounted on a horse trained like this; it was the cause of his death, since Onesilus's squire chopped the horse down with a scythe between the shoulders as it was rearing up over his master. And what the Italians report — that at the battle of Fornova the horse of Charles VIII, kicking and plunging, freed his master from the enemies pressing on him, without which he would have been killed — sounds like an enormous piece of luck, if it is true.

[In the narrative which Philip de Commines has given of this battle, in which he himself was present (lib. viii. ch. 6), he tells us of wonderful performances by the horse on which the king was mounted. The name of the horse was Savoy, and it was the most beautiful horse he had ever seen. During the battle the king was personally attacked, when he had nobody near him but a valet de chambre, a little fellow, and not well armed. "The king," says Commines, "had the best horse under him in the world, and therefore he stood his ground bravely, till a number of his men, not a great way from him, arrived at the critical minute."]

The Mamelukes boast that they have the most responsive horses of any cavalry in the world: by nature and training they are taught to recognise the enemy and to fall on him with mouth and hoofs at a word or sign, and also to pick up javelins and lances scattered on the field with their teeth and present them to their riders on command. It is said both of Caesar and of Pompey that, among their other excellent qualities, they were both very fine horsemen — and of Caesar in particular that in his youth, mounted on a bare back, without saddle or bridle, he could make a horse run, stop, turn, and go through all its paces with his hands behind him. Just as nature meant to make of this man, and of Alexander, two military miracles, she seems to have done her utmost to fit them out with extraordinary mounts as well: everyone knows that Alexander's horse Bucephalus had a head shaped a bit like a bull's, would let no one mount him or handle him but his master, and was so honoured after his death that a city was founded in his name. Caesar likewise had a horse whose forefeet looked like a man's, the hoofs divided like fingers, which would also let no one but Caesar ride him, and to whom, after the horse's death, he dedicated a statue to the goddess Venus.

I do not willingly dismount once I am on horseback, for it is the place where, well or ill, I am most at ease. Plato recommends it for health, and Pliny says it is good for the stomach and the joints. Let us go a little further with the subject, since here we are.

We read in Xenophon a law forbidding anyone who owned a horse to travel on foot. Trogus Pompeius and Justin say the Parthians used to perform all offices and ceremonies on horseback — not only in war but in every public and private affair, making bargains, holding conferences, entertaining, taking the air — and that the great distinction between freemen and slaves was that the one rode while the other went on foot, an institution founded by King Cyrus.

There are several examples in Roman history (Suetonius particularly notes it of Caesar) of captains who, in pressing situations, ordered their cavalry to dismount — both to cut off any hope of flight and because of the advantage they expected from this kind of fighting.
"Quo baud dubie superat Romanus,"
["Wherein the Roman does questionless excel."--Livy, ix. 22.]
says Livy. And so the first thing they did to head off mutinies and uprisings among newly conquered peoples was to take away their arms and horses, which is why we so often meet in Caesar:
"Arma proferri, jumenta produci, obsides dari jubet."
["He commanded the arms to be produced, the horses brought out, hostages to be given."--De Bello Gall., vii. II.]
To this day the Grand Signior allows no Christian or Jew to keep a horse of his own anywhere in his empire.

Our ancestors, especially in their wars with the English, fought most of their major engagements and pitched battles on foot, so as to have nothing but their own strength, courage, and steadiness to rely on in a quarrel involving life and honour. You stake — whatever Chrysanthes in Xenophon says to the contrary — your valour and your fortune on that of your horse; his wounds or death put you in the same danger; his fear or his fury can have you written off as rash or cowardly; if he has a hard mouth or refuses the spur, your honour pays for it. And so I do not find it strange that those foot-battles were more firmly fought and fiercer than the ones fought on horseback:
"Caedebant pariter, pariterque ruebant Victores victique; neque his fuga nota, neque illis."
["They fought and fell pell-mell, victors and vanquished; nor was flight thought of by either."--AEneid, x. 756.]
Their battles were much better contested. These days there is nothing but routs:
"Primus clamor atque impetus rem decernit."
["The first shout and charge decides the business."--Livy, xxv. 41.]

And the means we use in so dangerous a moment should be as much under our own control as possible. So I would advise choosing the shortest sort of weapons, the ones whose use we can best account for. A man can rely more on a sword he holds in his hand than on a bullet he fires from a pistol, where so many things have to come together for it to do its work — the powder, the flint, the wheel — and the failure of any one of them puts your fortune at risk. A man himself strikes much surer than the air can carry his blow:
"Et, quo ferre velint, permittere vulnera ventis Ensis habet vires; et gens quaecumque virorum est, Bella gerit gladiis."
["And so where they choose to carry [the arrows], the winds allow the wounds; the sword has strength of arm: and whatever nation of men there is, they wage war with swords."--Lucan, viii. 384.]

But I will say more about that weapon when I come to compare ancient arms with those in modern use. In passing: once the shock to the ear has worn off — which any man gets used to in no time — I take the firearm to be a weapon of very little effect, and hope we will one day lay it aside. The missile weapons the Italians used to use, with fire and with the sling, were much more terrifying. They had a kind of javelin tipped with an iron three feet long, made to pierce an armed man through and through, called the Phalarica. They sometimes threw it by hand on the field, sometimes shot it from various engines in the defence of besieged places. The shaft was wrapped round with flax, wax, rosin, oil, and other combustibles, which caught fire in flight, and landing on a man's body or shield, took away all use of arms and limbs. And yet, in close combat, I should think they would have damaged the attacker too, and that a camp planted with these flaming clubs would be a common nuisance to the whole crowd:
"Magnum stridens contorta Phalarica venit, Fulminis acta modo."
["The Phalarica, launched like lightning, flies through the air with a loud rushing sound."--AEneid, ix. 705.]

They had besides other devices that practice made them expert in (and that seem incredible to us who have never seen them) by which they got the same effects as our powder and shot. They threw their spears with such force as to transfix two shields and two armed men at once, and pin them together. And the work of their slings was no less certain or shorter in range:

["Culling round stones from the beach for their slings; and with these practising over the waves, so as from a great distance to throw within a very small circuit, they became able not only to wound an enemy in the head, but hit any other part at pleasure."--Livy, xxxviii. 29.]
Their siege batteries had not only the effect but the thunder of our cannon too:
"Ad ictus moenium cum terribili sonitu editos, pavor et trepidatio cepit."
["At the battery of the walls, performed with a terrible noise, the defenders began to fear and tremble."--Idem, ibid., 5.]
The Gauls, our kinsmen in Asia, hated these treacherous missile weapons; they preferred to fight bravely hand to hand:

["They are not so much concerned about large gashes — the bigger and deeper the wound, the more glorious do they esteem the combat — but when they find themselves tormented by some arrow-head or bullet lodged within, but presenting little outward show of wound, transported with shame and anger to perish by so imperceptible a destroyer, they fall to the ground."--Livy, xxxviii. 21.]

A pretty description of something very like a musket-shot. The ten thousand Greeks on their long and famous retreat met a nation that gave them a lot of trouble with great strong bows, shooting arrows so long that, if you picked one up, you could throw it back like a javelin and pierce through both shield and armed man. The engines Dionysius invented at Syracuse, to shoot huge solid darts and stones of enormous size with such force and to such a distance, came very close to our modern inventions.

But while we are on the subject of horses and horsemanship, we must not forget the comical figure cut by one Maistre Pierre Pol, a doctor of divinity, on his mule. Monstrelet reports that he always rode side-saddle, like a woman, through the streets of Paris. He says elsewhere that the Gascons had wonderful horses that could wheel at full speed — which the French, Picards, Flemings, and Brabanters regarded as a miracle, "never having seen the like before," in his own words.

Caesar, on the Suebi: "In the charges they make on horseback," he says, "they often throw themselves down to fight on foot, having taught their horses not to budge from the spot in the meantime, to which they then run back as needed; and by their custom, nothing is so unmanly and base as to use saddles or pads, and they despise anyone who does — so much so that, though only a few in number, they have no fear of attacking many." Something I used to wonder at — seeing a horse handled through all his paces with only a switch and the reins laid on his neck — was an everyday thing among the Massylians, who rode their horses with neither saddle nor bridle:
"Et gens, quae nudo residens Massylia dorso, Ora levi flectit, fraenorum nescia, virga."
["The Massylians, mounted on the bare backs of their horses, bridleless, guide them by a mere switch."--Lucan, iv. 682.]
"Et Numidae infraeni cingunt."
["The Numidians guiding their horses without bridles."--AEneid, iv. 41.]
"Equi sine fraenis, deformis ipse cursus, rigida cervice et extento capite currentium."
["The career of a horse without a bridle is ungraceful; the neck extended stiff, and the nose thrust out."--Livy, xxxv. II.]

King Alfonso, the one who founded the Order of the Band, or Scarf, in Spain, included among the rules of the order that members were never to ride a mule or a mulet, on penalty of a mark of silver — I had this lately from Guevara's Letters. Whoever called those the Golden Epistles had a very different opinion of them than I do. The Courtier says that until his day it was a disgrace to a gentleman to ride such a creature; but the Abyssinians, on the contrary, the closer they are to the person of Prester John, prefer to ride on great mules as the highest mark of dignity and rank.

Xenophon tells us the Assyrians had to keep their horses fettered in the stable because they were so fierce and bad-tempered, and that loosing and harnessing them took so long that, to avoid the disorder this slow preparation might cause if they were surprised, they never camped before fortifying the camp well with ditches and ramparts. His Cyrus, who was so great a master of horse service, kept his horses to their full daily work and never let them have anything to eat until they had earned it by the sweat of some kind of exercise. The Scythians, on campaign and short of food, used to bleed their horses, drink the blood, and live on that diet:
"Venit et epoto Sarmata pastus equo."
["The Scythian comes, who feeds on horse-flesh."--Martial, De Spectaculis Liber, Epigr. iii. 4.]
The people of Crete, besieged by Metellus, were so desperate for drink that they had to quench their thirst with their horses' urine.

To show how much more cheaply the Turkish armies keep themselves than our European ones, it is said that, besides drinking only water and eating nothing but rice and salted, pulverised meat (of which any man can easily carry a month's supply on his person), they know how to feed on the blood of their horses, like the Muscovites and Tartars, and salt it for their own use.

These newly discovered peoples of the Indies, when the Spaniards first landed among them, had so high an opinion of the men and the horses both that they took the first for gods and the second for animals raised above their natural kind. So much so that after they were subdued, when they came to sue for peace and pardon and to bring gifts of gold and provisions, they never failed to offer the same to the horses, with the same kind of speech they had made to the men, taking their neighing for a language of truce and friendship.

In the other Indies, riding an elephant was the first and royal place of honour; second came riding in a coach drawn by four horses; third, riding a camel; and last and lowest, being carried or pulled by only one horse. One of our recent writers tells us he has been in places out there where they ride oxen with pads, stirrups, and bridles, and very comfortably.

Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, in a battle with the Samnites, seeing that his horse had failed three or four times to break into the enemy's battalion, hit on this course: he had them unbridle all the horses and spur them as hard as they could go, so that with nothing to check their career, they would open a way for his foot through both weapons and men. By that means he handed the enemy a bloody defeat. The same order was given by Quintus Fulvius Flaccus against the Celtiberians:

["You will do your business with greater advantage of your horses' strength, if you send them unbridled upon the enemy, as it is recorded the Roman horse to their great glory have often done; their bits being taken off, they charged through and again back through the enemy's ranks with great slaughter, breaking down all their spears."--Idem, xl. 40.]

The Duke of Muscovy was once bound to pay this homage to the Tartars: when they sent an embassy to him, he went out to meet them on foot and presented them with a cup of mare's milk (their most highly prized drink), and if a drop happened to fall in drinking onto their horse's mane, he was obliged to lick it off with his tongue. The army Bajazet sent into Russia was overtaken by so terrible a snowstorm that, to shelter from the cold, many of them killed and disembowelled their horses and crawled into the bellies to enjoy the vital heat. Bajazet himself, after the savage battle in which Tamerlane overthrew him, had a fair chance of saving his own person on the speed of an Arabian mare he was riding, had he not been forced to let her drink her fill at a river ford on the way, which left her so heavy and sluggish that those pursuing him easily caught up. They do say that letting a horse stale takes the edge off him, but as for drinking I should have thought it would have refreshed him.

Croesus, marching his army across some wastelands near Sardis, ran into an infinite number of snakes, which the horses devoured with great appetite — and which Herodotus says was a prodigy of ill omen for his affairs.

We call a horse "entire" when he has his mane and ears whole; no other will pass muster. The Lacedaemonians, after defeating the Athenians in Sicily, returning in triumph to the city of Syracuse, among other insolences, had all the horses they had captured shorn and led in the procession. Alexander fought a nation called the Dahae, whose discipline was to ride two and two armed on a single horse to the war; in the fighting one of them would dismount, and so they fought, one on horseback and one on foot, taking turns.

I do not think that for graceful riding any nation in the world matches the French. In our way of speaking, a "good horseman" seems to refer more to the man's courage than to his skill in riding. Of all the horsemen I have seen, the most knowing in the art, the one with the best seat and the best method of breaking horses, was Monsieur de Carnavalet, who served our King Henry II.

I have seen a man ride standing with both feet on the saddle, take the saddle off and put it back on as he went, riding the whole time at full speed; gallop over a cap and make very good shots back at it with his bow; pick anything up from the ground with one foot on the ground and the other in the stirrup, and twenty other monkey tricks he made his living by.

In my time there have been seen at Constantinople two men on one horse who, at the height of the gallop, would throw themselves out of and back into the saddle by turns; one who bridled and saddled his horse with nothing but his teeth; another who, between two horses, with one foot on each saddle and a second man on his shoulders, would ride at full career, while the other stood bolt upright on him making very good shots with his bow; several who would ride at full speed with their heels up and their heads on the saddle, between drawn scimitars with the points fixed upwards in the harness. When I was a boy, the Prince of Sulmona, riding an unbroken horse in Naples that was ready for any trick, held coins under his knees and toes, as if they had been nailed there, to show the firmness of his seat.

title: Of ancient customs
paragraphs: I would gladly forgive our people for taking no pattern or rule of perfection but their own particular manners and customs — for it is a common vice, not just of the common run but of nearly all men, to walk in the beaten road their ancestors trod before them. I am content that, when they see a Fabricius or a Laelius, they think his face and bearing barbarous, since he is neither dressed nor groomed in our manner. But what I find fault with is their singular thoughtlessness in letting themselves be so blinded and bullied by the authority of present fashion that they change their opinions every month, if custom requires it, and revise their judgments on questions that touch them personally. When they wore the busk of their doublets up to their breasts, they stiffly insisted that was its proper place; a few years later, when it had slipped down between the thighs, they could laugh at the old fashion as uncomfortable and unbearable. The fashion now in use leads them to condemn both of the other two with such firm conviction and such universal consent that you would think a kind of madness had crept in among them, blinding their understanding to this strange degree. Now, given that our turnover of fashions is so prompt and abrupt that all the tailors in the world cannot dream up enough new whim-whams to feed our vanity, it must often happen that the discarded styles come back in again, and then drop into the same contempt; and that the same judgment, in fifteen or twenty years, will pass through half a dozen not only different but contradictory opinions, with an unbelievable lightness and inconstancy. Not one of us is so discerning as not to be taken in by this contradiction and, both in external and internal sight, blinded without realising it.

I want to muster up some old customs here that I still carry in my head, some of them the same as ours, others very different — so that, bearing in mind this constant variation in human things, we may have our judgment settled more clearly and firmly.
The thing we practice of fighting with rapier and cloak was practised by the Romans too:
"Sinistras sagis involvunt, gladiosque distringunt,"
["They wrapt their cloaks upon the left arm, and drew their swords."--De Bello Civili, i. 75.]

says Caesar; and he notes a bad custom of our nation that is still with us — stopping travellers we meet on the road to make them say who they are, and taking it as an insult and just cause of a quarrel if they refuse.

At the baths, which the ancients used every day before dinner, as routinely as we wash our hands, they at first only bathed their arms and legs. But later on, by a custom that has held in most nations for ages, they bathed completely naked in mixed and scented water, regarding it as a great crudity to bathe in plain water. The most delicate and affected perfumed themselves all over three or four times a day. They often had their body hair plucked off — as the women of France have lately taken to doing with their foreheads —
"Quod pectus, quod crura tibi, quod brachia veilis,"
["You pluck the hairs out of your breast, your arms, and thighs."--Martial, ii. 62, i.]
though they had ointments suited to the purpose:
"Psilotro nitet, aut acids latet oblita creta."
["She shines with unguents, or with chalk dissolved in vinegar."--Idem, vi. 93, 9.]
They enjoyed soft sleeping, and cited lying on a mattress as proof of toughness. They ate reclining on couches, much as the Turks do today:
"Inde thoro pater AEneas sic orsus ab alto."
["Thus Father AEneas, from his high bed of state, spoke."--AEneid, ii. 2.]

And it is said of the younger Cato that after the battle of Pharsalia, sinking into melancholy at the bad state of public affairs, he always ate sitting, taking up a strict and austere way of life. It was also their custom to kiss the hands of great men as a mark of honour and affection. And in greeting friends, they always kissed in salutation, as the Venetians still do:
"Gratatusque darem cum dulcibus oscula verbis."
["And kindest words I would mingle with kisses."--Ovid, De Pont., iv. 9, 13]

In petitioning or saluting any great man, they used to lay their hand on his knee. Pasicles the philosopher, brother of Crates, instead of placing his hand on the knee laid it on the private parts. When the man he had thus saluted roughly pushed him away, Pasicles said: "What — is not that part as much your own as the other?" They ate fruit, as we do, after dinner. They wiped themselves (let the ladies, if they like, find a daintier way of putting it) with a sponge, which is why spongia is a smutty word in Latin; the sponge was fixed to the end of a stick, as appears from the story of the man who, as he was being led off to be thrown to the wild beasts in full view of the people, asked leave to relieve himself, and having no other way to do himself in, shoved the sponge and stick down his throat and choked himself. After sex they used to wipe with perfumed wool:
"At tibi nil faciam; sed Iota mentula lana."
They had vessels and little tubs in the streets of Rome for passers-by to urinate in:
"Pusi saepe lacum propter se, ac dolia curta. Somno devincti, credunt extollere vestem."
["The little boys in their sleep often think they are near the public urinal, and raise their coats to make use of it."--Lucretius, iv.]

They took refreshments between meals, and in summer they kept cellars of snow to cool their wine. Some used snow even in winter, finding their wine still not cold enough at that cold time of year. People of quality had their cupbearers and carvers, and their buffoons to entertain them. They had their meat served in winter on chafing dishes set on the table, and they had portable kitchens (I have seen some myself) that they carried about, with all their service inside:
"Has vobis epulas habete, lauti Nos offendimur ambulante caena."
["Do you, if you please, esteem these feasts: we do not like the ambulatory suppers."--Martial, vii. 48, 4.]

In summer they had a device for bringing fresh, clear streams through their ground-floor rooms, in which they kept plenty of live fish, which the guests drew out with their own hands to have each cooked to his liking. Fish has always had this advantage, and still keeps it, that the great pretend to be cooks where fish are concerned; and indeed the taste is more delicate than that of meat, at least to my palate. But in every sort of magnificence, debauchery, and indulgent invention of effeminacy and expense, we do, frankly, all we can to match them — for our appetites are as corrupt as theirs were; we just lack the means to keep up. Our strength is no more able to reach them in their vicious qualities than in their virtuous ones, because both came from a vigour of soul incomparably greater in them than in us; and the weaker souls are, the less they can do either very well or very badly.

The place of honour among them was the middle. Going first or coming last, in writing or in speaking, carried no signal of higher rank, as their writings make plain: they will as readily say Oppius and Caesar as Caesar and Oppius, and me and thee as thee and me. This is what once made me notice, in the life of Flaminius in our French Plutarch, a passage where the author, speaking of the jealous quarrel over honour between the Aetolians and Romans about the winning of a battle they had jointly won, seems to make something of the fact that in the Greek songs the Aetolians had been placed before the Romans — assuming there is no ambiguity in the French translation.
Ladies, at the baths, made no fuss about admitting men, and even had their menservants rub and anoint them:
"Inguina succinctus nigri tibi servus aluta Stat, quoties calidis nuda foveris aquis."
["A slave--his middle girded with a black apron--stands before you, when, naked, you take a hot bath."--Martial, vii. 35, i.]
They all dusted themselves with a certain powder to keep the sweat down.
The ancient Gauls, says Sidonius Apollinaris, wore their hair long in front and shaved at the back — a fashion that is starting to come back in this vicious and effeminate age.
The Romans paid the boatmen their fare as they stepped into the boat, which we never do until we have landed:
"Dum aes exigitur, dum mula ligatur, Tota abit hora."
["Whilst the fare's paying, and the mule is being harnessed, a whole hour's time is past."--Horace, Sat. i. 5, 13.]
Women used to lie on the wall side of the bed, which is why they called Caesar
"Spondam regis Nicomedis,"
["The bed of King Nicomedes."--Suetonius, Life of Caesar, 49.]
They took breath in their drinking, and they watered their wine:
"Quis puer ocius Restinguet ardentis Falerni Pocula praetereunte lympha?"
["What boy will quickly come and cool the heat of the Falernian wine with clear water?"--Horace, Od., ii. z, 18.]
And the cheeky looks and gestures of our lackeys were known among them too:
"O Jane, a tergo quern nulls ciconia pinsit, Nec manus, auriculas imitari est mobilis albas, Nec lingua, quantum sitiat canis Appula, tantum."

["O Janus, whom no crooked fingers, simulating a stork, peck at behind your back, whom no quick hands deride behind you, by imitating the motion of the white ears of the ass, against whom no mocking tongue is thrust out, as the tongue of the thirsty Apulian dog."--Persius, i. 58.]
The Argive and Roman ladies mourned in white, as ours used to do — and as they still should, were I to have my way in this matter. But there are whole books on the subject.

title: Of Democritus and Heraclitus
paragraphs: Judgment is a tool of universal use, and pushes in on every subject — which is why, in these Essays, I take hold of any occasion that offers itself. Even when the subject is one I do not really understand, I still try it out, sounding it from a distance; and finding it too deep for my height, I keep to the shore. This very knowledge that one can go no further is one of the effects of judgment's virtue — and one of those it is most proud of. Sometimes I try, on an idle and frivolous subject, to find material from which to compose a body and then prop it up; sometimes I employ judgment on a noble subject, one that has been tossed and tumbled by a thousand hands, where a man can hardly bring anything of his own to bear, the path being so beaten on every side that he must necessarily walk in another man's footsteps. In such a case, judgment's task is to pick the way that seems best, and out of a thousand paths to determine that this or that is the best. I leave the choice of my topics to chance and take the first one that presents itself; they are all the same to me, since I never plan to treat any of them exhaustively. I never see all of anything — neither do those who promise so freely to show all of it to others. Of the hundred limbs and faces every thing has, I take one, one time merely to look it over, another time to scrape its skin, sometimes to pinch it to the bone. I make one thrust — not wide, but as deep as I can — and I am most often tempted to take a thing in hand by some new light I notice in it. If I knew myself less well, I might risk going to the bottom of something or other and being deceived by my own incapacity; but as it is, sprinkling a word here and a word there, patterns cut from different pieces and scattered without design, without committing myself too far, I am not answerable for them or bound to stay on my subject; I vary at my own liberty and pleasure, surrendering to doubt and uncertainty and to my own governing method, which is ignorance.

All motion reveals us. The very same soul of Caesar that showed itself so plainly in marshalling and commanding at Pharsalia showed itself just as busily in the softer affairs of love and leisure. You judge a horse not only by seeing him show off his paces, but by his everyday walk — even by seeing him stand in the stall.

Among the soul's functions there are some of a lower and humbler grade; whoever does not see her in those lesser offices as well as in the grander ones never sees her fully. Indeed, she is perhaps best seen where her step is plainest. The winds of the passions catch her most when she is flying highest, the more so because she throws herself wholly into, and brings her whole virtue to bear on, every single subject, never handling more than one thing at a time, and handling it not according to itself but according to her. Things in themselves perhaps have their own weight, measures, and conditions; but once we take them into us, the soul shapes them as she likes. Death is terrible to Cicero, longed for by Cato, a matter of indifference to Socrates. Health, conscience, authority, knowledge, wealth, beauty, and their opposites all strip themselves at the door of the soul and put on a new robe, of another cut — and of whatever colour the soul pleases, brown, bright, green, dark — and of whatever quality, sharp, sweet, deep, or superficial. They are not agreed on any common standard of form, rule, or procedure: each soul is a queen in her own kingdom. Let us, then, stop excusing ourselves on the strength of the external qualities of things; it is up to us to give an account of them. Our good and our ill depend on nothing but ourselves. That is where our offerings and our vows are owed, not to fortune — she has no power over our character. On the contrary, character drags her along in its train and casts her in its own mould. Why should I not judge Alexander at table, raving and drinking at the prodigious rate he sometimes did?

Or judge him by his game of chess? What string of his soul was not touched by that idle, childish game? I hate and avoid it, precisely because it is not play enough — it is too grave and serious a diversion, and I am ashamed to put as much thought and study into it as would serve much better uses. He did not pump his brains harder over his glorious expedition into the Indies, nor does any other man poring over a passage on which the safety of mankind hangs. To what a pitch does that ridiculous distraction grip the soul, when all her faculties are summoned for this trivial business — and what a fine opportunity it gives every man to know himself and judge himself rightly! I do not put myself more thoroughly through the sieve in any other posture. What passion are we spared in it? Anger, spite, malice, impatience, and a violent desire to win in a contest where it would be more excusable to be ambitious of being beaten — for to stand out, to excel above the common rate in frivolous things, does not suit a man of honour. What I say of this example may be said of all the others. Every particle, every employment of a man, shows him just as much as any other.

Democritus and Heraclitus were two philosophers of whom the first, finding the human condition ridiculous and empty, never appeared in public except with a mocking and laughing face; while Heraclitus, taking pity on that same condition of ours, always appeared with a sorrowful look and tears in his eyes:
"Alter Ridebat, quoties a limine moverat unum Protuleratque pedem; flebat contrarius alter."
["The one always, as often as he had stepped one pace from his threshold, laughed, the other always wept."--Juvenal, Sat., x. 28.]

I am clearly on the side of the first humour — not because it is more pleasant to laugh than to weep, but because it carries more contempt and condemnation than the other; and I think we can never be despised as much as we deserve. Pity and lament seem to imply some esteem and value for the thing pitied, whereas the things we laugh at are by that very act declared to be of no weight. I do not think we are as unhappy as we are vain, or as malicious as we are foolish; we are not so full of mischief as of emptiness, nor so wretched as we are vile and mean. And so Diogenes, who passed his time rolling about in his tub and thought nothing of the great Alexander, holding us no better than flies or bladders puffed with wind, was a sharper and more piercing judge — and, in my opinion, a juster one — than Timon, called the Man-hater. For what a man hates he takes to heart. Timon was an enemy of all mankind, who passionately wished our ruin and avoided our company as dangerous, coming as it did from wicked and corrupt natures. The other valued us so little that we could neither trouble nor infect him by our example; he left us to herd together among ourselves, not out of fear but out of contempt for our society, judging us as incapable of doing good as of doing evil.

Of the same stamp was Statilius's answer when Brutus tried to draw him into the conspiracy against Caesar: he agreed the enterprise was just, but he did not think mankind worth a wise man's trouble — in line with the doctrine of Hegesias, who said a wise man should do nothing except for himself, since he alone deserved it, and with the saying of Theodorus, that it is not reasonable a wise man should risk himself for his country, or endanger wisdom for a pack of fools. Our condition is as ridiculous as it is laughable.

title: Of the vanity of words
paragraphs: A rhetorician of old said his profession was to make little things look great. He was a shoemaker who could make a great shoe for a small foot. At Sparta they would have had a man like that whipped for openly claiming to practise a sly and deceitful craft, and I suspect Archidamus, who was king there, was a little taken aback by Thucydides' answer when he asked him who was the better wrestler, Pericles or himself. Thucydides replied that it was hard to say: "For when I have thrown him," he said, "he always persuades the spectators that he never fell, and walks off with the prize." Women who paint, powder, and plaster over their ruins, filling in their wrinkles and blemishes, are less to blame, because it hardly matters whether we see them in their natural complexions; these orators, on the other hand, make a business of deceiving not just our sight but our judgement, and of adulterating and corrupting the very essence of things. Republics that have held themselves to a steady and well-ordered government, like Sparta and Crete, kept orators in very low esteem. Aristo wisely defined rhetoric as "a science for persuading the people"; Socrates and Plato called it "an art of flattery and deception." Even those who deny the description in general confirm it throughout in their precepts. The Muslims will not let their children be taught the art, judging it useless; and the Athenians, seeing how pernicious its practice had become — for in their city it was universally admired — ordered the principal part of it, the rousing of the emotions through opening and closing flourishes, to be cut out. It is a contraption invented for managing and steering a disorderly and turbulent crowd, and is no more used in a healthy state than medicine is used in a healthy body — only when things are out of joint. In states where the populace, or the ignorant, or both together, have been all-powerful and able to give the law — Athens, Rhodes, Rome — and where public affairs have been in a constant storm of upheaval, the orators have always flocked. And in truth we find few men in those republics who rose to any great eminence without the help of eloquence.

Pompey, Caesar, Crassus, Lucullus, Lentulus, Metellus drew from it their chief means of climbing to the heights of authority they finally reached, finding it more useful than arms — contrary to the opinion of better times. For when L. Volumnius spoke publicly in favour of electing Q. Fabius and Publius Decius to the consulship, he said: "These are men born for war and great in action; in the combat of the tongue, total amateurs; spirits truly consular. The subtle, the eloquent, the learned are only good for the city, to make praetors of, to administer justice."

Eloquence flourished at Rome most when public affairs were in the worst state and most troubled by internal upheaval — as a free, uncultivated soil bears the rankest weeds. From which it would seem that a monarchical government has less need of it than any other. For the stupidity and pliability natural to common people, which makes them so easy to turn, twist, and lead by the ears through the charming harmony of words without any weighing of the truth and reality of things by reason — that pliability is not easily found in a single person, and it is also easier by good upbringing and counsel to keep him from the impression of this poison. No famous orator was ever known to come out of Persia or Macedon.

I have launched into this subject because of an Italian I lately took into my service, who had been clerk of the kitchen to the late Cardinal Caraffa until his death. I asked the fellow to give me an account of his old office, and he set to expounding this palate-science with such a composed expression and magisterial gravity, as though he were handling some deep point of theology. He drew a learned distinction between the different sorts of appetites: the one a man has before he begins to eat, and those that come after the second and third courses; the means of simply satisfying the first, and then of stirring and awakening the other two; the ordering of the sauces, first in general, then going on to the qualities of the ingredients and their effects; the differences between salads according to season, which should be served hot, which cold; the manner of dressing and decorating them so they would be pleasing to the eye. After which he moved on to the order of the whole service, full of weighty and important considerations:
"Nec minimo sane discrimine refert, Quo gestu lepores, et quo gallina secetur;"

["Nor with less discrimination does it matter how we should carve a hare, and how a hen," or, ("Nor with the least discrimination does it tell how we should carve hares, and how cut up a hen.") — Juvenal, Sat., v. 123.]
and all this delivered in lofty and magnificent words, the very same we use when we discuss the government of an empire. This learned lecture from my man brought to mind these lines of Terence:

"Hoc salsum est, hoc adustum est, hoc lautum est, parum: Illud recte: iterum sic memento: sedulo Moneo, qux possum, pro mea sapientia. Postremo, tanquam in speculum, in patinas, Demea, Inspicere jubeo, et moneo, quid facto usus sit."

["This is too salt, that's burnt, that's not washed enough; that's well; remember to do it that way next time. So I am always advising them to have things done properly, to the best of my judgement; and finally, Demea, I tell my cooks to look into every dish as into a mirror, and I instruct them what needs doing." — Terence, Adelph., iii. 3, 71.]

And yet even the Greeks themselves greatly admired and loudly praised the order and arrangement Paulus Aemilius laid on at the feast he gave them on his return from Macedon. But I am not talking here about the deeds; I am talking only about the words.

I do not know whether it works on other men the way it works on me, but when I hear our architects thunder out their pompous terms — pilasters, architraves, cornices, Corinthian and Doric orders, and the rest of the jargon — my imagination is at once filled with the palace of Apollidon; and then, after all, I find they are talking about the cheap fittings of my own kitchen door.

When you hear men talk of metonymies, metaphors, allegories, and other words out of the grammar books, would you not think they were referring to some rare and exotic form of speech? And yet these are turns of phrase very close to the chatter of my chambermaid.

Of the same stamp is the trick of giving the offices of our kingdom the lofty titles of the Romans, though they bear no resemblance in function, still less in authority and power. And the same goes for what I fear will one day count as a reproach to our age: the cheap, indiscriminate granting of the most glorious surnames antiquity bestowed on only one or two men across several centuries. Plato carried off the surname Divine by such universal consent that no one ever grumbled at it or tried to take it from him; and yet the Italians, who claim — and with good reason — sharper wits and sounder sense than the other nations of their time, have lately conferred the same title on Aretino, in whose writings, apart from inflated phrases set out in clever periods (ingenious, yes, but far-fetched and outlandish), and whatever quality his eloquence has, I see nothing that lifts him above the ordinary writers of his time, let alone anything that approaches that ancient divinity. And we now think nothing of giving the surname Great to princes who have nothing in them above the ordinary.

title: Of the parsimony of the ancients
paragraphs: Attilius Regulus, commander of the Roman army in Africa at the height of all his glory and his victories over the Carthaginians, wrote to the Republic to inform them that a certain hired man he had left in charge of his estate — which came in all to no more than seven acres — had run off with all his farming tools, and to beg them to please call him home so he could see to his own affairs, lest his wife and children should suffer for it. The Senate appointed someone else to manage his business, made good his losses, and ordered his family to be maintained at the public expense.

The elder Cato, returning as consul from Spain, sold his warhorse to save the cost of shipping it back by sea to Italy. As Governor of Sardinia he made all his visits on foot, with no other attendance than one officer of the Republic, who carried his robe and a censer for sacrifices, and for the most part he carried his trunk himself. He boasted that he had never owned a gown costing more than ten crowns, nor ever sent above tenpence to the market for a day's provisions, and that none of his country houses was even rough-cast on the outside.

Scipio Aemilianus, after two triumphs and two consulships, went on an embassy with no more than seven servants in his train. They say Homer had only one, Plato three, and Zeno, founder of the Stoic school, none at all. Tiberius Gracchus, while serving as public minister on the affairs of the state, was allowed only fivepence halfpenny a day — and at that moment he was the greatest man in Rome.

title: Of a saying of Caesar
paragraphs: If we would sometimes spend a little thought on ourselves, and use the time we waste prying into other men's actions and into things outside us to examine our own capacities instead, we would soon see what frail and decaying material this fabric of ours is made of. Is it not a striking proof of our imperfection that we cannot settle our satisfaction on any one thing, and that even our own fancy and desire rob us of the power to choose what is most fitting and useful for us? A good demonstration is the unending dispute among the philosophers about finding man's sovereign good — a dispute still going and likely to go on forever, with no solution and no agreement.
"Dum abest quod avemus, id exsuperare videtur Caetera; post aliud, quum contigit illud, avemus, Et sitis aequa tenet."
["While the thing we want is missing, it seems to surpass everything else; then, once we have it, we want something else, and the same thirst keeps hold of us." — Lucretius, iii. 1095.]

Whatever falls into our knowledge and our possession, we find it does not satisfy, and we keep panting after things to come and unknown — since what is present does not suffice us. Not, in my judgement, that they lack what would do the job, but because we lay hold of them with an unruly and immoderate haste:

"Nam quum vidit hic, ad victum qux flagitat usus, Et per quae possent vitam consistere tutam, Omnia jam ferme mortalibus esse parata; Divitiis homines, et honore, et laude potentes Aflluere, atque bona natorum excellere fama; Nec minus esse domi cuiquam tamen anxia corda, Atque animi ingratis vitam vexare querelis Causam, quae infestis cogit saevire querelis, Intellegit ibi; vitium vas efficere ipsum, Omniaque, illius vitio, corrumpier intus, Qux collata foris et commoda quomque venirent."

["For when he saw that nearly everything required for survival, and everything that could make life secure, is already laid out for mortals' hands — that men have abundant wealth, honour, praise, and the joy of children with a good name, and yet for all that no one's heart at home is free of anxieties, his mind worn down by ungrateful complaints — he understood that the vessel itself was at fault, and that all the good things brought into it from outside were spoiled by its own defects." — Lucretius, vi. 9.]

Our appetite is unsteady and fickle; it can neither hold nor enjoy anything with any grace. Man, deciding the fault lies with the things he possesses, fills himself with — and feeds on — the idea of things he neither knows nor understands; on these he hangs his hopes and his desires, paying them all reverence and honour, in the spirit of Caesar's saying:
"Communi fit vitio naturae, ut invisis, latitantibus atque incognitis rebus magis confidamas, vehementiusque exterreamur."
["It is the common vice of nature that we put the most trust in, and feel the greatest fear of, things unseen, hidden, and unknown." — De Bello Civili, xi. 4.]

title: Of vain subtleties
paragraphs: There is a class of little tricks and frivolous subtleties from which men sometimes hope to earn reputation and applause — like the poets who compose whole poems with every line beginning with the same letter. We see the shapes of eggs, globes, wings, and hatchets cut out by the ancient Greeks by the measure of their verses, lengthened or shortened to make this or that figure. Of this kind was the labour of the man whose business it was to count up how many different orders the letters of the alphabet could be transposed in, and who arrived at the incredible total Plutarch reports. I am very taken with the spirit of the man,

["Alexander, as may be seen in Quintilian, Institut. Orat., bk. ii., ch. 20, where he defines Maratarexvia as a certain unnecessary imitation of art, which really does neither good nor harm but is as pointless and ridiculous as the labour of the man who had so perfectly learned to throw small peas through the eye of a needle at a good distance that he never missed one, and was justly rewarded for it, as the story goes, by Alexander, who watched the performance, with a bushel of peas." — Coste.]

who, when a man was brought before him who had learned to throw a grain of millet with such dexterity and surety that he never missed the eye of a needle, and who was afterwards begged to give something as a reward for so rare a feat, ordered — pleasantly, and in my view quite justly — a certain number of bushels of the same grain to be delivered to him, so he would not lack what to practise so famous an art on. It is a strong sign of weak judgement when men admire things just because they are rare and new, or because they are difficult, without any merit or usefulness joined to recommend them.

I have just come from playing with my own family at a game of finding the most things that touch at both extremities. "Sire," for instance, is a title given to the greatest man in the nation, the king, and also to the lowliest, like merchants — but never to anyone of any rank in between. Women of high birth are called Dames, lesser gentlewomen Demoiselles, and the meanest sort of women Dames again, like the first. The cloth of state above our tables is allowed only in the palaces of princes and in taverns. Democritus said that gods and beasts have sharper senses than men, who are in the middle. The Romans wore the same clothes at funerals and at feasts. It is quite certain that extreme fear and an extreme rush of courage both equally trouble and loosen the bowels. The nickname "the Trembling" by which they called Sancho XII, king of Navarre, tells us that valour will set the limbs trembling just as fear does. Those who were arming that king — or whoever else, on a like occasion, was apt to fall into the same agitation — tried to settle him down by playing down the danger he was about to face. "You don't understand me," he said, "for if my flesh could know the danger my courage will straight away carry it into, it would sink to the ground."
