The faintness that overtakes us in the exercises of Venus, from coldness or distaste, also comes from too violent a desire and an immoderate heat. Extreme cold and extreme heat both scald and roast. Aristotle says that lead pigs will melt and run with cold and the harshness of winter just as with a strong heat. Desire and satiety fill all the gradations above and below pleasure with pain. Stupidity and wisdom meet at the same midpoint of feeling and resolution in the bearing of life's accidents: the wise master and triumph over ill, the others never know it; the latter, you might say, sit on this side of the accidents, the former go beyond them, having weighed and considered their character, measured and judged them for what they are, and then, by force of a vigorous soul, leapt out of their reach; they look down on them and trample them underfoot, having a solid and well-fortified soul against which the darts of fortune, when they come to strike, must necessarily rebound and blunt themselves, meeting a body in which they can make no impression. The ordinary middling sort of men are lodged between these two extremes, made up of those who notice their evils, feel them, and are not able to bear them. Infancy and decrepitude meet in the weakness of the brain; avarice and prodigality meet in the same thirst and desire to get.

One could say, with some show of truth, that there is a beginner's ignorance that comes before knowledge, and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it — an ignorance that knowledge creates and brings forth at the same moment that it dispatches and destroys the first. Out of average understandings, little curious and little instructed, are made good Christians, who by reverence and obedience simply believe and stay constant in their belief. In the middling understandings and the average sort of capacities, the error of opinion is bred; they follow the look of the first impression and have some colour of reason on their side to charge us with simplicity and stupidity for walking on in the old beaten path — meaning those of us who have not informed ourselves by study. The higher and nobler souls, more solid and more clear-sighted, make up another sort of true believers, who by a long and religious investigation of truth have gained a clearer and more penetrating light into the Scriptures, and have uncovered the mysterious and divine secret of our ecclesiastical polity; and yet we see some who, going by the middle step, have reached that highest degree with marvellous results and confirmation, arriving at the outer limit of Christian intelligence and enjoying their victory with great spiritual consolation, humble acknowledgement of divine favour, reform of manners, and singular modesty. With these I do not mean to rank the others who, to clear themselves of any suspicion of their former errors and to satisfy us that they are sound and firm, become extremely indiscreet and unjust in the pressing of our cause, and disgrace it with endless reproaches of violence and oppression. The plain peasants are good people, and so are the philosophers, or whatever the present age calls them — men of strong and clear reason, whose souls are enriched with a full instruction in profitable sciences. The mongrels, who have despised the first form of the ignorance of letters and have not been able to reach the other (sitting between two stools, as I and many more of us do), are dangerous, foolish, and a nuisance; these are the ones who trouble the world. And that is why I, for my part, retreat as far as I can back towards the first and natural station, which I so vainly tried to advance from.
Popular and purely natural poetry
["The term poesie populaire was used, for the first time, in the French language on this occasion. Montaigne coined the expression and indicated its nature." — Ampere.]

has in it certain artless graces by which she may stand comparison with the greatest beauty of poetry brought to perfection by art — as we see in our Gascon villanelles and in the songs that come to us from peoples who know nothing of any science, not even the use of writing. The middling sort of poetry, between these two, is despised, with no value, honour, or esteem.

But seeing that once a path is opened to the fancy, I have found — as commonly happens — that what we had taken for a difficult exercise and a rare subject turns out to be nothing of the kind, and once the invention warms up it finds out an endless number of parallel examples. I shall only add this: that if these Essays of mine were worth a serious critical judgement, it might then, I think, turn out that they would not much take with common and vulgar minds, nor be very welcome to the singular and excellent sort of men; the first would not understand them enough, and the last too much; so they may hover in the middle region.

title: Of smells
paragraphs: It has been said of some — as of Alexander the Great — that their sweat gave off a fragrant smell, the result of some rare and extraordinary constitution into the cause of which Plutarch and others have inquired. But the ordinary constitution of human bodies is quite otherwise, and their best and chief excellence is to be free of any smell at all. Even the sweetness of the purest breath has nothing more perfect about it than to be without any offensive smell, like the breath of healthy children — which is what made Plautus say of a woman:
"Mulier tum bene olet, ubi nihil olet."
["She smells sweetest who does not smell at all." — Plautus, Mostellaria, i. 3, 116.]
And those who go in for fine exotic perfumes are with good reason to be suspected of some natural defect they are trying to cover up with these scents. To smell, even sweetly, is to stink:
"Rides nos, Coracine, nil olentes Malo, quam bene olere, nil olere."
["You laugh at us, Coracinus, because we have no scent; I would rather, than smell well, not smell at all." — Martial, vi. 55, 4.]
And elsewhere:
"Posthume, non bene olet, qui bene semper olet."
["Posthumus, the man who always smells well does not smell well." — Idem, ii. 12, 14.]
I am, even so, a great lover of good smells, and equally a hater of bad ones, which I also catch from a greater distance, I think, than other men:
"Namque sagacius unus odoror, Polypus, an gravis hirsutis cubet hircus in aliis Quam canis acer, ubi latest sus."
["My nose is quicker to scent a foul sore or a rank armpit than a sharp dog is to smell out a hidden sow." — Horace, Epod., xii. 4.]

Of smells, the simple and natural ones seem to me the most pleasing. Let the ladies look to it, for it is mostly their concern. In the deepest barbarism, the Scythian women, after bathing, used to powder and crust their faces and their whole bodies with a certain fragrant drug that grew in their country, and when this was cleaned off and they came to be with their men, they were found perfumed and silky. It is hard to believe how strangely all sorts of odours cling to me, and how readily my skin takes them up. The man who complained that nature had not given mankind a vehicle to carry smells to the nose had no reason for it — they do that on their own, especially in my case. My moustache, which is thick, does the office for me: if I stroke it with my gloves or handkerchief, the smell will not leave it the whole day; it tells where I have been. And the close, sweet, devouring, viscid, melting kisses of youthful ardour in my wanton age left a sweetness on my lips for hours afterwards. And yet I have always found myself little subject to the epidemic diseases that are caught either by contact with the sick or bred by the contagion of the air, and have escaped those of my time, several sorts of which have visited our cities and our armies. We read of Socrates that though he never left Athens during the frequent plagues that ravaged the city, he alone was never infected.

Physicians could, I believe, draw more use out of odours than they do, for I have often noticed that they cause an alteration in me and work on my spirits according to their several qualities; which leads me to approve of what is said — that the use of incense and perfumes in churches, so ancient and so universally taken up in all nations and religions, was intended to cheer us, to rouse and purify the senses, and so the better to fit us for contemplation.

I would have liked, the better to judge of it, to have tasted the culinary art of those cooks who had so rare a way of seasoning exotic odours with the relish of meats — as was particularly noted in the service of the king of Tunis, who in our day landed at Naples for an interview with the Emperor Charles. His dishes were larded with fragrant drugs to such an expense that the dressing of one peacock and two pheasants amounted to a hundred ducats; and when the carver came to cut them up, not only the dining room but every apartment of the palace and the streets nearby were filled with an aromatic vapour that did not soon disperse.

My chief concern in choosing lodgings is always to avoid a thick and stinking air; and those beautiful cities, Venice and Paris, lose much of my fondness for them — the one through the offensive smell of her marshes, the other through her dirt.
